slides.title:
Find defective parts
before they ship
slides.body:
Use real circuit-board photos to compare detectors, review their mistakes, and save a version another engineer can reproduce.
Three hours · CPU classifiers · your own Forge project
slides.notes: The inspection team is fictional. The VisA PCB1 images, masks and recorded comparisons are real. Do not promise that every participant run improves.

slides.title: The factory has two ways to waste a good morning
slides.body:
A defect gets through

A board with a missing or damaged component passes inspection.

A good board gets held

An inspector spends time checking a normal board that the detector rejected.

Management has requested fewer of both. It has not supplied a third category called “probably fine.”
slides.notes: Ask participants which cost matters in their own work. We will count both errors. The joke does not define the release threshold.

slides.title: What is in the teaching set?
slides.body:
1,104 photographs

One PCB family. 1,004 normal boards and 100 defective boards.

Image labels

A board-level normal or defective label is the classifier target.

Defect masks

Annotations let us inspect mistakes. They never enter the classifier.

VisA, Zou et al. · CC BY 4.0 · the provided supervised split is preserved
slides.notes: Explain the distinction between detecting a defective board and locating its defect. This classifier does the former. A patch-distance heatmap is not a segmentation model.

slides.body:
Notebook step: Inspect the boards.
  1. Click Download and verify the PCB1 teaching data.
  2. Choose a training board. Explain what would make you inspect it.
  3. Turn on Reveal the published defect label and mask.
Check: Describe the annotated region without treating the mask as an input to your detector.
slides.notes: This is a participant decision, not a model evaluation. Give people a minute to make their own assessment before discussion.

slides.title: Compare each patch with real normal examples
slides.body:
First recipe

Compare a patch with the average normal patch at that location.

An average can fall between different normal appearances.

Follow-up recipe

Find the closest actual normal training patch at that location.

Training cases cannot match themselves.

The same reference bank is used for validation and test. Those boards never enter the bank.
slides.notes: This is the concrete mechanism we changed after the first recipe failed its AP gate. It is not a universal claim about nearest neighbors.

slides.title: Add local information to the classifier
slides.body:
Notebook step: Compute image features.
  1. Complete build_features: calculate patch errors, apply np.log1p, and flatten one row per board.
  2. Append the patch values to the whole-image vector along axis 1.
  3. Click Check my patch-feature function.
Check: The check preserves board order and verifies both whole-image and nearest-patch behavior.
slides.notes: The learner function is passed into fitting and saved with the freeze. Final evaluation reloads that saved source, not the current draft.

slides.title: Check the feature cache without rebuilding everything
slides.body:
```python weights = teaching.fetch_weights(weights_path) result = teaching.recompute_batch(data_root, weights) assert result["matching_cached_features"] ```
Optional button: Recompute four cached board features. Downloads pinned weights; no model-provider call.
slides.notes: The retained lossless inputs allow exact feature comparison. The prepared full cache took 39.25 seconds on the preparation Mac using two Torch CPU threads. This is not an attendee timing guarantee.

slides.title: Train the same classifier on each representation
slides.body:
```python {1-4|6|all} model = inspection.fit_classifier( data, fit_rows, method, build_features=build_features, C=0.03, ) validation_scores = inspection.score(data, validation_rows, model) ```
C controls regularization. This worked recipe fixes C before your run; labels and training cases are the same.
slides.notes: Do not describe this as training a vision foundation model. We fit a logistic classifier over fixed encoder outputs. Patch distances add features but do not use pixel masks.

slides.title: A detector score still needs an operating rule
slides.body:
Lower threshold

Flag more boards. Usually catch more defects and create more false alarms.

Higher threshold

Flag fewer boards. Some defects can pass unnoticed.

Review band

Send uncertain cases to people. Report that extra workload separately.
slides.notes: Scores are decision values, not calibrated defect probabilities. The optional review margin is in score units. A valid threshold function does not make the policy safe.

slides.title: Implement the validation threshold
slides.body:
Notebook step: Compare global and patch features.
  1. In choose_threshold, sort the scores of known validation defects.
  2. Choose the largest cutoff that still catches at least 90% of them.
  3. Click Check my threshold function, then Train both feature representations.
Check: Compare misses and false alarms alongside average precision.
slides.notes: Allow participants to finish the local check before training. The 90 percent requirement constrains recall on validation only, not a guarantee for the final set.

slides.title: Keep ranking quality and operating errors separate
slides.body:
MeasureQuestion it answers
Average precisionAre defective boards ranked ahead of normal boards?
Misses and false alarmsWhat happens at the frozen threshold?
Review volumeHow many decisions are handed to a person?
slides.notes: AP summarizes precision over recall levels. Do not compare it to accuracy or confuse a change in review volume with better detection.

slides.body:

slides.title: Worked answer: assemble the local features
slides.body:
```python whole = data["whole"][rows] if method == "whole": return whole errors = inspection.nearest_patch_errors(data, rows, reference) local = np.log1p(errors).reshape(len(rows), -1) return np.concatenate([whole, local], axis=1) ```
The notebook answer also supports the historical mean-patch method used in the free fixture.
slides.notes: Use the complete notebook answer for the local check. The input has one row per board; axis 1 appends features.

slides.title: Worked answer: meet the validation recall target
slides.body:
```python positives = np.sort(scores[target == 1])[::-1] position = int(np.ceil(recall * len(positives))) - 1 return float(positives[position]) ```
At 12 validation defects and recall .90, keep the top 11 above the threshold.
slides.notes: The retained cutoff depends on validation examples. It does not guarantee the same recall on final boards.

slides.title: Worked answer: choose uncertain cases
slides.body:
```python rng = np.random.default_rng(seed) order = rng.permutation(len(rows)) order = order[np.argsort( np.abs(scores[order] - threshold), kind="stable" )] return np.asarray(rows)[order[:budget]] ```
The permutation only breaks equal-distance ties. Do not pass labels to this function.
slides.notes: Active selection here is uncertainty sampling. It is one policy to test, not a proven universal choice.
